transcripts.question: Give me Luke’s 30-second overview: who he is, what he’s shipped, and why it matters.
transcripts.raw:
I'm a product designer who combines research, systems thinking, technical prototyping, and business judgment to ship useful products — currently finishing a CS degree at BYU.

- **Pitch** [/work/pitch](/work/pitch): current contract work (design + engineering) redesigning the whole rep app for an AI sales coach, now live with a pilot team.
- **Lucid** [/work/lucid-ai](/work/lucid-ai): shipped the Lucid AI assistant to general availability in 12 weeks.
- **Awardco** [/work/awardco-login-flow-redesign](/work/awardco-login-flow-redesign): redesigned login/auth, validated in usability testing (25% faster logins, 4.5% more successful sign-ins), handed off after my internship.
- **Pattern** [/work/pattern-custom-reports](/work/pattern-custom-reports): redesigned Custom Reports, validated in 24 usability sessions, handed off at internship's end.

My read is the common thread is pairing research with technical fluency to make real tradeoff calls, not just mockups.

Which project best shows your judgment?
What shipped at Lucid in 12 weeks?
What are you building at Pitch right now?

transcripts.question: Walk me through a difficult product decision Luke made: the tradeoff, what he chose, and how it played out.
transcripts.raw:
The one that stands out is the Awardco login redesign.

In task testing with 75 people, password-first was actually faster (4.6 seconds vs 5.9) and scored slightly higher on confidence. The easy call would've been to ship the faster design.

I chose SSO-first anyway, because a year of telemetry showed password login only succeeded 34.6% of the time in the real product — the fastest option in testing was the one most likely to fail people in production.

In before-and-after usability testing, the SSO-first system produced a 25% faster login and a 4.5% increase in successful sign-ins, alongside a 78% reduction in login-method decision time.

**Why it matters:** I weighted real failure data over a usability-test win on speed alone.

The design was validated and handed off after my internship; I don't have post-launch numbers.

[Awardco](/work/awardco-login-flow-redesign)

[[followups]]
What was validated before the Awardco handoff?
Why did you choose the slower login design at Awardco?
What tradeoff did you make at Pattern?

transcripts.question: Did Luke reduce Awardco’s failed logins by 4.5%?
transcripts.raw:
Not quite — the 4.5% figure is a different metric, in a different direction.

In before-and-after usability testing of the redesigned Awardco login system, we saw a 4.5% increase in successful sign-ins, not a reduction in failed logins. That testing also showed a 25% faster login and a 78% reduction in login-method decision time (27 seconds down to 5.9 seconds), with higher confidence and lower reported difficulty.

The 7.7 million failed login attempts (6.7 million from password login) are from the year of telemetry that motivated the redesign in the first place — that's the baseline problem, not an outcome I measured.

**Why it matters:** the telemetry showed people choosing the wrong authentication method, not mistyping passwords, which is why the redesign identifies users by email and routes them to the method most likely to work.

The redesign was validated in testing and handed off at the end of my internship, so I don't have production numbers either way.

[Awardco](/work/awardco-login-flow-redesign)

[[followups]]
Why did you choose the slower login design at Awardco?
What was validated before the Awardco handoff?
What did the SSO token flow solve?

transcripts.question: What happened after Awardco launched?
transcripts.raw:
Here's the correction: Awardco didn't launch, at least not that I know of. What I can tell you is where things stood when my internship ended.

The redesign was validated in usability testing and I handed off the completed designs for implementation after my internship wrapped. That included the SSO-first flow, the token-based login I took through security review, the SMS verification for deskless workers, and the reset flow improvements.

I don't have any post-launch or production data for Awardco — no numbers on whether it went live, when, or what happened to login success or support cases afterward. The only measured results I can point to are from before-and-after usability testing: a 25% faster login, a 4.5% increase in successful sign-ins, and a 78% reduction in decision time, all from testing, not production.

More detail on the handoff is in [Awardco](/work/awardco-login-flow-redesign).

transcripts.question: Did Pattern test with 24 daily users?
transcripts.raw:
Not quite — I ran 24 usability sessions with 12 brand managers and 12 advertising strategists, and I only have them by role, not by how often they used the product.

Those sessions were where I tested the redesigned Custom Reports flows. The results from that testing: participants built a client-ready report in under 10 minutes (against a 30–60 minute baseline across Predict, Excel, and slides), and satisfaction ratings came in 50% higher than for the old tool — both in usability testing, not production.

The redesign was validated through that testing and handed off at the end of my internship. I don't have any data on what happened to it after that.

You can read the full story in [Pattern](/work/pattern-custom-reports).

[[followups]]
What was the most important change testing produced at Pattern?
What did you hand off at Pattern?
What tradeoff did you make at Pattern?

transcripts.question: What was Lucid AI’s adoption rate?
transcripts.raw:
That one isn't in my portfolio, so I won't guess at it. My internship ended shortly after the external release on August 5, so I don't have long-term adoption data.

What I can speak to: the assistant went from a blank page to general availability in 12 weeks, reached internal users on July 20 ahead of the wider release, and shipped with four core skills — Find docs, Summarize, Build a diagram, and Catch up — narrowed down from more than 20 capabilities I prototyped and tested. I also ran 12 external user sessions during development.

Before I left, I designed and implemented an A/B test comparing a side-panel and full-page version of the assistant, meant to measure which capabilities performed best — but I don't have those results either, since it ran after I was gone.

If adoption numbers matter for what you're evaluating, the closest thing I have is the [Lucid](/work/lucid-ai) case study itself, which walks through the research and design decisions in detail.
